prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

When setting street trees, full consideration shall be given to their relative relationship with traffic signs, information boards, etc. The spacing between trees in front of traffic signs and information boards may be increased to around 18 m. Where obstruction has already formed in the existing condition, trees shall be pruned according to actual conditions, or the position, style, and height of the signs shall be adjusted. 3.3 Median strips 3.3.1 Design 1. Definition The green partition between carriageways; the one located between the upstream and downstream motor vehicle lanes is the central median; the one located between motor vehicle lanes and non-motorized lanes or between motor vehicle lanes in the same direction is the side median. 2. Layout forms A. Central median a. The central median of urban arterial roads with a design speed higher than 60 km/h shall be densely planted with evergreen plants to avoid glare interference from oncoming traffic at night. 70 b. Within the range of 0.6 m to 1.5 m above the surface of the adjacent motor vehicle roadway, the plants configured shall have dense foliage throughout the year, and their spacing shall not be greater than 5 times the canopy spread. c. The width of the central median shall be 1.5 m or more, and a formal arrangement structure shall be adopted; simple repetition is preferable to create rhythm. At intersections and important nodes, plants shall mainly be low shrubs; planting trees is strictly prohibited to avoid tree trunks causing glare and traffic accidents. justice: The street allocates most visible space to multiple wide motor-vehicle lanes, while pedestrian space is pushed to the far edge on the right, suggesting an uneven distribution of street resources for all road users.

A planted median and side greenery create some separation and environmental benefit, but there is no visible dedicated space for cyclists or clearly marked pedestrian priority areas, limiting fairness across travel modes.

Accessibility appears limited because the sidewalk is distant and partially obscured by trees and planting strips, and no visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossings can be confirmed in the image.
safety: Lane markings are clear and the carriageway is wide and orderly, which supports predictable vehicle movement and reduces immediate conflict between cars.
The landscaped median separates opposing traffic streams, lowering the risk of head-on conflicts and improving overall road safety for drivers.
Streetlights are regularly spaced and roadside trees are set back from the travel lanes, helping maintain a relatively controlled roadside environment and preserving sight lines.
livability: The corridor feels dominated by fast-moving traffic and long travel distances, with little visible street-level activity such as shops, seating, or social spaces that would support everyday public life.
Trees and planted medians add greenery and soften the road environment, which improves the setting somewhat for all users.

The visible sidewalk on the right is separated from traffic by a planted strip, but it appears secondary to the roadway and does not show amenities that would make the street socially active or inviting.
sustainability: Continuous rows of trees and planted medians provide urban greenery, which can support shade, air-quality improvement, and ecological value.
The broad roadway design still prioritizes private motor traffic with several general-purpose lanes, which weakens the street's sustainability performance.
No visible bus stop, transit lane, or bicycle lane can be identified, so support for lower-carbon travel modes is not evident in the image.
aesthetics: The avenue has a clean, orderly appearance with consistent lane markings, evenly spaced light poles, and maintained planting strips.
Rows of mature and semi-mature trees on the right side create a greener and more visually pleasant edge than a fully hardscaped roadway would.
The central median planting and overall symmetry of the boulevard contribute to a coherent and attractive visual composition.
comfort: Tree cover along the right side offers some shade potential for the sidewalk zone, which can improve thermal comfort for people outside vehicles.
The roadway surface appears smooth and well maintained, supporting physical comfort for drivers and reducing vibration from poor pavement.
Psychological comfort is mixed: the corridor is visually open and uncluttered, but the large scale of the road and dominance of moving cars can feel less comfortable for non-motorized users.
walkability: A sidewalk is visible on the right side, but it is set far from the main roadway and there are no visible crosswalks, pedestrian signals, or curb ramps to show easy pedestrian connectivity.
The street section is very wide and vehicle-oriented, which increases crossing difficulty and reduces convenience for walking across or along the corridor.

Although trees improve the walking environment somewhat, the absence of visible benches, active frontages, and pedestrian-priority features limits the street's attractiveness and practicality for walking.

As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort

- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

When setting street trees, full consideration shall be given to their relative relationship with traffic signs, information boards, etc. The spacing between trees in front of traffic signs and information boards may be increased to around 18 m. Where obstruction has already formed in the existing condition, trees shall be pruned according to actual conditions, or the position, style, and height of the signs shall be adjusted. 3.3 Median strips 3.3.1 Design 1. Definition The green partition between carriageways; the one located between the upstream and downstream motor vehicle lanes is the central median; the one located between motor vehicle lanes and non-motorized lanes or between motor vehicle lanes in the same direction is the side median. 2. Layout forms A. Central median a. The central median of urban arterial roads with a design speed higher than 60 km/h shall be densely planted with evergreen plants to avoid glare interference from oncoming traffic at night. 70 b. Within the range of 0.6 m to 1.5 m above the surface of the adjacent motor vehicle roadway, the plants configured shall have dense foliage throughout the year, and their spacing shall not be greater than 5 times the canopy spread. c. The width of the central median shall be 1.5 m or more, and a formal arrangement structure shall be adopted; simple repetition is preferable to create rhythm. At intersections and important nodes, plants shall mainly be low shrubs; planting trees is strictly prohibited to avoid tree trunks causing glare and traffic accidents. Figure 3.3-1 Schematic diagram of central median B. Side median a. Where the width of the side green belt between carriageways is greater than or equal to 1.5 m, trees shall be the main planting type, and trees, shrubs, and groundcover plants should be combined. The canopies of trees on both sides should not overlap above the motor vehicle lanes. b. Where the width of the side green belt between carriageways is less than 1.5 m, shrubs shall be the main planting type, and shrubs and groundcover plants should be combined. 71 Figure 3.3-2 Schematic diagram of central median C. Characteristic island heads a. Quality enhancement of island-head flower borders and landscape stones shall be carried out on the premise of not affecting driving sight distance, not obstructing traffic signs, signal monitoring facilities, or lighting effects. b. It is encouraged to set up Suzhou-specific rockery stones and pruned topiary forms, creating a regional garden-style landscape with varied stone forms, distinct layers of vegetation, and brightly colored flowers. c.
